items.content:
Tankers defy Iran attacks to keep crude oil flowing through Hormuz
More commercial ships, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack in October than at any other point in the Iran war.
But tankers continue to ship substantial volumes of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz, in stark contrast to March when exports cratered due to Iranian attacks.
Shippers have adapted to wartime in the Persian Gulf but at a very high cost.
Rapidan Energy's McNally: Ceasefire optimism is fading and crude is repricing
Within 24 hours of the U.S. and Israel going to war with Iran, Tehran responded with a wave of attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz to cut off one of the world's main sources of crude oil.
Iran's campaign was initially successful, with crude exports plunging nearly 90% to 1.8 million barrels a day in March compared with 16 million bpd in February, according to data provided by Kpler.
But crude flows have rebounded over the past eight months as the U.S. military provides protection to tankers transiting Hormuz. Tehran has responded by escalating its attacks in recent weeks .
More commercial ships have come under attack in October than at any other point in the war. Yet in contrast to March when exports cratered, tankers have continued to ferry substantial volumes of crude oil through Hormuz in a sign that the shipping industry has adapted to wartime in the Persian Gulf.
As of Oct. 27, at least 30 vessels, mostly oil tankers, were hit this month leaving at minimum 16 seafarers injured, according to data from the International Maritime Organization , a United Nations agency. Ship attacks doubled in October compared with 15 confirmed incidents in September.
"It's a difficult situation. Ships are attacked really on a daily basis," said Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at Denmark-headquartered BIMCO, one of the big international shipping trade associations.
Ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz surged in October
Crude prices have surged more than 13% this month as security conditions have deteriorated in the Persian Gulf. The international Brent contract traded above $117 a barrel on Friday. That's just shy of its wartime closing high of $118.35 during Iran's big wave of ship attacks in March.
Yet actual crude exports through Hormuz stood at nearly 11.1 million bpd on average in October, only about 2% lower from September despite the sharp escalation of violence, Kpler's data shows.
"On balance in terms of oil coming out, there hasn't been a massive impact," said Mary Melton, senior tanker analyst at Braemar, a ship broker headquartered in London.
Crude flows through Hormuz are highly volatile on a daily basis with exports near prewar levels one day while falling well below such levels another day. The final leg of October has seen flows decline to 7.3 million bpd for the week ended Wednesday, more than 40% below the prewar baseline, according to Kpler.
Oil flows are more resilient now because the shipping industry has adjusted its operations to the threats, Larsen said. Freight rates have soared, making it "more attractive for the risk takers in the industry to actually carry out these voyages," he said.
"And when the cost of oil goes up that also means that there's more commercial incentives to get the oil out and sell it in the global market," Larsen said.
Shippers have adapted by setting up a shuttle system to reduce the risk of attack. Tankers load crude at Persian Gulf ports, sail through Hormuz with their transponders turned off and transfer the cargo to tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman that then deliver it to refiners in Asia. This reduces insurance costs for the ships waiting outside the strait, Melton said.
The shuttle system has been effective at getting oil out with flows through Hormuz surging more than 70% since July, according to Kpler. But this system is also inefficient, logistically complicated and expensive, Melton said.
It requires more equipment, ships and experienced crews, the analyst said. About 20% of the world's supertanker fleet is tied up helping to shuttle oil out of the Gulf, she said.
Tanker rates have exploded as a consequence. It cost $249,000 per day to hire a supertanker to make the journey from the Gulf of Oman to Asia in early September, Melton said. By the first week of October, the price had surged to more than $900,000 per day. This translates to about $21 in transportation costs per barrel of crude oil compared with $6.50 a barrel in September, the analyst said.
"If you're an importer in Asia, you're used to paying almost nothing for freight," Melton said. "Then you're facing 20% to 30% of the actual delivered cost of crude is going to freight.
"That really starts impacting your margins as a refiner," the analyst said.
More Gulf oil producers are now covering the cost and risk of shipping through Hormuz in a bid to claw back market share in Asia from the U.S. and other Atlantic producers, she said. And they are increasingly using their own tankers to run the gauntlet through the strait, she said.
It is unclear how long the complex and expensive shuttle system can sustain current export levels. The tankers transiting Hormuz are totally dependent on air support from the U.S. military for their security, Larsen said.
"I don't think there would be many shipowners willing to take the risk if they didn't have that air cover from U.S. fighter jets and helicopters and drones," he said.
It is also uncertain how long the U.S. military will remain engaged, particularly if Democrats regain control of Congress after Tuesday's elections and demand that the president end the war.
The U.S. has told several Gulf Arab nations to be ready for a short but intense military campaign following the Nov. 3 midterm elections, people briefed on the conversations told The Wall Street Journal . The U.S. Navy, which is enforcing a blockade against Iran, has warned ships that don't need to transit the Persian Gulf, Hormuz and Gulf of Oman to steer clear of the region.
"Due to the current geopolitical situation, vessels which do not need to transit the area are advised to remain well clear to avoid unnecessary delays to their voyage," the U.S. military told vessels Wednesday through a notice issued by the Joint Maritime Information Center .

items.summary: Trump says Iran war will end soon, US military insists Hormuz is secure  アラブニュース
items.content:
Trump says Iran war will end soon, US military insists Hormuz is secure
Trump says Iran war will end soon, US military insists Hormuz is secure
US president says there will be no military strike against Iran prior to elections
Commander of US military in Middle East says he did not see any Iranian military presence in Strait of Hormuz
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said on Friday that he ‌believed the ‌war with ‌Iran will end soon despite reports that the US and Israel are planning a fresh round or strikes.
“It's going to get wrapped ‌up ‌soon,” Trump ‌said in ‌an interview with a Kansas City radio station as he campaigned ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“We ‌need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Trump has said the US would not strike Iran before the elections, with the conflict proving a key issue during campaigning.
His comments come amid a wave of diplomacy in the region to try and break the stand-off coupled with reports of a possible new military campaign against Iran once the midterms are finished.
The US military’s senior officer overseeing the Middle East, Adm. Brad Cooper, met Trump at the White House on Thursday to outline military options in Iran, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The US-Iran war has become focussed on shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz where Iran attempted to stop energy exports from the region in response to the initial US-Israeli attacks.
Washington has managed to create a protected shipping route through the strait, which has allowed oil shipments to climb back to their pre-war levels despite ongoing Iranian attacks.
At the same time, the US says it has completely cut off oil exports from Iran with its own blockade.
Cooper, the head of the Pentagon's Central Command, said on Friday that during a recent flight he took over the Strait of Hormuz there was no Iranian military presence because “Iran’s Navy is all at the bottom of the sea.”
“I saw dozens of commercial vessels transiting. All types. Cargo, crude oil, liquid natural gas, or LNG,” Cooper said in a video.
“I didn’t see the IRGC out there, at all,” he added.
He said US forces were ensuring the strait’s shipping lanes remained free from Iranian sea mines after a major operation to remove the devices.
The US military says it has helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer.
Despite the progress, Iran continues to attack ships making the journey.
Oman said on Friday it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship that was targeted and set ablaze in the waterway. Iran reported three oil tankers were halted while transiting.
Meanwhile, a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials.
The visit took place a day after Iran said it had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance addressed to security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
The Wall Street Journal said the letter focused on a possible framework for negotiations.
Earlier in the week, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkike – members of the Makkah defense alliance – flew to Tehran for talks.

items.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
items.summary: The American-made interceptors are the only effective weapon for downing Russia's ballistic missiles.
items.content:
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.
However Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (Â£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies which his country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.

, Global Desk Last Updated: Oct 30, 2026, 09:36:00 PM IST
Why is the US stock market down today? Weak earnings from Intel and Amazon, plus AI worries, pulled the Nasdaq down 2.14% and the S&P 500 down 1.29%. Dow Jones is at 52,113.50, down 0.44%. Nvidia, AMD and Reddit also fell.
TIMESOFINDIA.COM US stock market today: Intel, Amazon, Nvidia and AMD slide, dragging the Dow, Nasdaq and S&P 500 lower on Friday
US stock market today: US stocks fell for the second day in a row on Friday, October 30, as investors worried about the health of the AI trade. At 10:58 AM ET, the Dow Jones was at 52,113.50, down 229.06 points or 0.44%. The S&P 500 was at 7,621.06, down 99.33 points or 1.29%. The Nasdaq was at 25,623.29, down 561.44 points or 2.14%.
Two earnings reports, from Amazon and Intel, came after Thursday’s closing bell and are pulling the market down this morning.
ALSO READ: Why Intel stock price down today? INTC shares plunged 29% today despite strong earnings - how the AI memory crunch and weak PC demand hit its forecast, and could the selloff deepen?
Thursday was already weak. All three major indexes closed lower, and the Nasdaq lost 1.6% after Alphabet’s results disappointed. Amazon and Alphabet both posted rare earnings misses. Alphabet had its worst day in over 20 years.
Amazon missed estimates on both revenue and profit. Its free cash flow also fell because of heavy spending on AI. Intel dropped sharply after giving a weak outlook for the fourth quarter.
Chip stocks fell across the board. AMD lost 9%, Marvell 6% and Broadcom 5%. Micron and Nvidia each gave up more than 3%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), which holds Intel and AMD as its two biggest positions, was down 7%.
Crypto stocks also took a hit. Bitcoin fell to around $76,600 from a high near $82,000 on Thursday. Strategy (MSTR) was down 10%, Coinbase (COIN) 12% and Robinhood (HOOD) 8%.
In other markets, WTI crude was above $104 a barrel, up about 2%. Gold fell to around $3,920, close to its lowest level since last November. The 10-year Treasury yield stayed at 4.94%.
Intel stock price today: why the chipmaker is down nearly 30%
Intel (INTC) is the worst performer on the S&P 500 today. At 10:58 AM ET it traded at $66.52, down $25.55 or 27.75%. Earlier in the session it fell about 30%, to below $65. That is a price the stock has not seen since spring.
The fall comes after a big run. Intel was up roughly 250% this year through Thursday’s close, and had recently crossed levels last seen in 2000.
The trigger was the company’s outlook. Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and GAAP profit of 10 cents a share. Both are below the average estimate tracked by Visible Alpha. This overshadowed third-quarter numbers that were better than expected. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company faces “headwinds across the PC industry” and is finding it hard to meet “extremely high AI driven demand.”
Intel’s foundry business, which makes chips for other companies, is also under watch. Its revenue rose nearly 60% year on year in Q3, but it posted an operating loss of nearly $1.9 billion.
Valuation is another worry. Before the fall, Intel traded at more than 50 times estimated 2027 earnings, well above its peer group average. Morgan Stanley, which rates the stock neutral, cut its price target to $75 from $84. The Visible Alpha average target is around $90.
High trending stocks today: Amazon, Nvidia, Reddit and more
Amazon (AMZN) traded at $239.31, down 1.84%. Third-quarter revenue rose nearly 12% from a year ago to about $202 billion. Net income fell, partly because last year’s quarter had gains from its stake in Anthropic. Amazon still expects AWS revenue growth run rates above 40% in both 2027 and 2028. The stock is up just 3% this year, while the S&P 500 is up 11%.
Nvidia (NVDA) was at $207.25, down 3%. Alphabet (GOOGL) was at $280.64, down 1.12%, and CoreWeave (CRWV) was at $55.48, down 8.65%. SpaceX (SPCX) was at $138.52, down 3.73%, and Nokia (NOK) was at $8.66, down 6.98%.
Three internet stocks also fell after their Q3 results. Reddit (RDDT) dropped 24%, Roblox (RBLX) 16% and Pinterest (PINS) 6%.
Acumen Pharmaceuticals (ABOS) fell 87.47% to $0.29.
A few stocks rose. TNL Mediagene (TNMG) gained 24.26% to $3.79 and Rivian (RIVN) added 5.41% to $12.07.

Federal Reserve officials are signaling more interest rate hikes to come
St. Louis Fed's Alberto Musalem calls for tightening soon, while Dallas Fed's Lorie Logan sees at least two quarter-point increases
By Cris Tolomia · 2 min read · Updated October 30, 2026
Two Federal Reserve officials said Friday that interest rates need to rise from their current level. The comments by St. Louis Federal Reserve Bank President Alberto Musalem and Dallas Federal Reserve Bank President Lorie Logan follow the Fed's decision this week to hold rates steady .
Musalem outlined his views in prepared remarks for the Shadow Open Market Committee in New York. “I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon,” he said. “Incremental adjustments made earlier are usually less disruptive than larger and abrupt actions taken later.”
Logan, in prepared remarks for Davidson College students , said the Federal Open Market Committee "needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases." She said she voted this week to maintain the target range of 3.75% to 4%. After the two increases, she said, the committee should hold off and take stock of how the economy and markets are evolving.
Logan said skipping a meeting "does not change the monetary policy destination." She estimated that the target range is at least 50 basis points below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring inflation back to target.
Musalem said inflation is "too high," with headline and core measures running at 3% or higher. He called the scenario in which inflation persists meaningfully above 2% without further removal of policy accommodation the more likely one. He described the labor market as stable and balanced around full employment, with unemployment at 4.2%.
Logan said core PCE inflation was 3.1% over the 12 months through September.
Taking questions afterward, Musalem said he is keeping a close eye on core inflation and looking for evidence that price pressures are spreading, according to CNBC . Logan is one of the officials who will cast a vote on the December rate decision, while Musalem will not have a vote on the committee until 2028.
The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.
The central bank raised rates by a quarter point in September, its first increase since July 2023 . Sixteen of 18 policymakers projected at least one more increase in that meeting's updated projections.
Musalem said on Oct. 9 that rates may need to rise over the next six to nine months.

items.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
items.summary: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
items.content:
Image source, Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images
By Rachel Clun Business reporter ,Â  Reporting from New York
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (Â£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

items.title: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars
items.summary: Global diesel prices surged as Ukraine and Iran struck refineries in Russia and the Middle East.
items.content:
Profits at the U.S. oil majors' refineries surged as they ramped up production to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices globally.
Diesel has surged as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants have attacked refineries in Russia and the Middle East.
ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods: We are producing record volumes of diesel in North America
Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices.
Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday.
The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. Importers have increasingly turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel supplies as a consequence.
ExxonMobil's profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street's expectations.
"Refining capacity is very tight today," Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. "Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand."
U.S. diesel stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA. Prices in the U.S. hit a record high in September.
Chevron's net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street's expectations of $4.89.
"The system is under stress," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. "We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile."
Here's what Chevron and Exxon earned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
Chevron earnings per share: $5.28 adjusted, vs. $4.89 expected
Chevron revenue: $67.8 billion, vs. $61.6 billion expected
Exxon earnings per share: $4.23 adjusted, vs. $4.08 expected
Exxon revenue: $113.2 billion, vs. $103.1 billion expected
High profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon "were making too much money based on a shortage." The supply disruption began in March after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.
Profits from Chevron's refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period.
Chevron CEO Mike Wirth on Venezuela licenses: Output to reach roughly 600k barrels per day by 2031
Chevron's U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said.
Exxon's refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business' earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025.
Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced "record volumes of diesel" in the quarter, Woods said.
Chevron's oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year.
Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025.

items.content:
A fire near Dubai international airport in March after a ‘drone-related incident’ set a fuel tank alight. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
A fire near Dubai international airport in March after a ‘drone-related incident’ set a fuel tank alight. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’
Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates . Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
Flights were suspended at Dubai’s international airport in March after the attack. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

Oman has rescued 25 crew members from a burning crude oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz as ships continue to be targeted in the besieged waterway .
The Omani Maritime Security Centre said in a statement on Friday that it had evacuated the people on board the RITI merchant ship. Oman said the vessel was flying the Panamanian flag, and the tracking website MarineTraffic identified it as a crude oil tanker.

The incident came as Iran said four tankers attempting to use “unauthorised routes” to cross the Strait of Hormuz were halted.
It is unclear whether one of the vessels was the tanker whose crew Omani maritime authorities evacuated.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said all four vessels were carrying oil and that the ships had been halted following “incidents” or after hitting mines.
“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement on Friday.
Hours later, the IRGC said two more tankers – each carrying more than two million barrels of oil – “exploded and caught fire” as a result of hitting mines while attempting to pass through an “unauthorised route”.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Navy said on Friday that it struck and destroyed an unmanned enemy craft to the east of the strait.
Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran’s permission.
It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to transit Hormuz without authorisation would face “destruction”.
Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28.
The US military denies the naval mine claims. On Friday, United States Central Command chief Brad Cooper said the Strait of Hormuz’s “internationally recognised primary transit routes” had been successfully cleared of Iranian sea mines.
Shipping in the Strait of Hormuz is operating at about 70 percent below pre-war levels, the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday.

items.title: Trump’s foreign policy, from Ukraine to Iran, raised fears of world war three. Americans are about to have their say - The Guardian
items.summary: Trump’s foreign policy, from Ukraine to Iran, raised fears of world war three. Americans are about to have their say  The Guardian
items.content:
‘In recent weeks, Trump – who pledged during his victorious 2024 presidential election campaign to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict within 24 hours of returning to office – appears to have abandoned Ukraine.’ Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images
‘In recent weeks, Trump – who pledged during his victorious 2024 presidential election campaign to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict within 24 hours of returning to office – appears to have abandoned Ukraine.’ Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images
Trump’s foreign policy, from Ukraine to Iran, raised fears of world war three. Americans are about to have their say
Voters who backed the US president in the last election are saying they can’t vote for him today: ‘This is an abomination’
Outside the Ukrainian educational and cultural center in a quiet Pennsylvania suburb of Jenkintown, on the outskirts of Philadelphia, a banner expressed unqualified gratitude: “Thank you USA for supporting Ukraine .”
Inside, however, the sentiment was altogether different. Irene Skulsky, a retired teacher in her late 70s, voiced indignation at Donald Trump ’s sudden turn against her ancestral homeland, which she believed had come close to killing her son, Darko, and a desire to punish his fellow Republicans at next week’s midterm elections.
“When we vote, we have to vote with Ukraine in our hearts,” she told her fellow retirees, gathered to hear a presentation by the Daughters of Knyahynya, a women’s group delivering military equipment to Ukrainian special forces on the frontline. “I know many people here are Republicans , but we can’t go according to party lines now. Ukraine needs us. They need our support. We need to shift the balance of power in Congress and in the Senate.”
Days earlier, Skulsky told fellow members at a meeting of the Ukrainian American Senior Citizens Association, Darko had been sitting in traffic en route to work in Kyiv when Russian drone missiles slammed into five cars immediately ahead of him.
There had been no prior alert, allegedly as a result of a decision by Washington to suspend its intelligence-sharing arrangement with Ukraine that has acted as an early warning system against missiles attacks since Russia invaded in February 2022.
In recent weeks, Trump – who pledged during his victorious 2024 presidential election campaign to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict within 24 hours of returning to office – appears to have abandoned Ukraine.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump during a meeting on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations general assembly in New York City, on 22 September. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images He struck a deal with the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, to buy nearly 5m tonnes of diesel, overriding US sanctions on Moscow. He called on Ukrainians to replace the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy . His administration was accused of throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service.
And while the Trump administration denied that it had stopped sharing intelligence this month, as relations with Ukraine nose-dived, Zelenskyy has said his country received no advance warning from US intelligence networks of two Russian missile attack waves.
Darko escaped injury, but several people in the vehicles in front were killed in the strikes, according to Skulsky. Her frustration spilled over to include Trump’s fellow Republicans, whom she said were “selling our souls” rather than standing up to the president.
“Republicans are afraid of Trump,” she said. “They’re afraid to lose their position. I think their heart is with Ukraine, but they’s sitting on their hands.”
Many American Ukrainians will express their outrage at the polls on 3 November, according to Eugene Luciw, a retired lawyer and local representative of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, an advocacy group.
“For [American] Ukrainians, I believe foreign policy is unquestionably the No 1 issue,” he said. “But I think even the average American without the added affinity of a homeland in Europe is going to see foreign policy as a very important issue.
“It’s beginning to reach people’s minds and hearts that something very important is brewing in Europe. If Ukraine loses this war, we have the beginnings of world war three.”
The most recent Ukraine development is the latest in a trio of Trump foreign policy decisions with the potential to hurt Republicans when Americans head to the polls next week.
More relevant to voters’ living costs – a key issue in this election, according to polls – has been Trump’s protracted war with Iran , and his determination to impose tariffs on imports from much of the world.
The Iran war, launched with Israel in February, shows no signs of ending despite Trump’s early claims that it would be a short-term “excursion” certain to end in the “unconditional surrender” of Tehran’s Islamic regime.
Instead, Trump has reportedly drawn up plans to launch renewed strikes against Iran after the midterms as he seeks to break Iran’s grip on the strait of Hormuz, an energy choke point that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies before the Tehran regime closed it in response to being attacked.
Gas and diesel prices at a Chevron gas station on 14 August in Fort Stockton, Texas. Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty Images The strait’s closure has resulted in soaring global oil prices, which have been passed on to US consumers in the form of higher prices for petrol and diesel, which is vital for supply chains and US farmers.
Polls have consistently shown voters’ disapproval of Trump’s handling of the war, and his management of the economy and inflation. Roughly 70% are now critical of both, according to a recent AP-Norc survey .
The war’s economic impact has compounded the inflationary effects of Trump’s tariffs, which has affected the prices of consumer goods and increased costs for manufacturers by increasing the costs of imported raw materials such as steel, copper and aluminum.
The tariff regime has also strained Washington’s relations with once-close allies – perhaps most visibly with Canada, the US’s second-biggest trading partner. Ties between the two neighbors plunged to a new low in August following the collapse of bilateral trade talks.
Following the collapse, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on $20bn of Canadian imports – including cars, forestry and dairy produce – triggering a retaliatory tit-for-tat response from Canada’s government, led by the prime minister, Mark Carney. In Michigan, which shares a border with Canada, even Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers released an ad calling on Trump to end the trade war and declared: “Canada is not our enemy.”
Trump has articulated his vision with characteristic bullishness. After January’s US attack on Venezuela, during which it ousted the country’s president, Nicolás Maduro , he dubbed his strategy the “Donroe doctrine” – a play on the Monroe doctrine, named after a 19th-century US president, which states that the western hemisphere should be Washington’s exclusive domain.
He bragged about extracting Venezuela’s oil resources and fantasized about making the country “the 51st state” in a speech this week in Corpus Christi, Texas, during which he showed off a tanker he claimed was carrying 1m barrels of oil and repeated a phrase – “to the victors belong the spoils” – that startled foreign leaders when he first uttered it at last month’s gathering of the United Nations general assembly.
There are fears that his neo-imperialist instincts could be applied after the midterms to Cuba, where he has repeatedly pledged to topple the communist regime that has ruled for the past 67 years.
Meanwhile, Trump’s fixation with autocratic leaders has been extended to China’s president, Xi Jinping. Having already met Xi at a summit in Beijing this year before hosting him at the White House, Trump will go to China again next month to meet the Chinese leader.
On a range of issues, he has shown disdain for diplomatic niceties – dispensing with seasoned diplomats to instead rely on Steve Witkoff, a real estate investor and attorney with no background in foreign policy, and Jared Kushner, his businessman son-in-law, as negotiators over matters as intricate as Iran, Gaza and Ukraine.
From left, Jared Kushner, Steve Witkoff and Volodymyr Zelenskyy after a joint news conference, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on 6 September. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Yet Trump’s latest Ukraine turn carries special resonance, not least because it risks a dramatic rupture with Washington’s European Nato allies, who are heavily invested in Kyiv’s protection as a first line of defence.
It has highlighted once again Trump’s complex relationship with Putin, an autocratic leader for whom he has repeatedly voiced admiration. It is also a reminder of Trump’s failure to live up to his frequently expressed vow to swiftly end the Ukraine war during the 2024 presidential election campaign.
Trump has blown hot and cold towards Zelenskyy. At an explosive White House meeting in February 2025, he told the Ukrainian leader “you don’t have the cards” – but with a peace deal on terms acceptable to Russia seeming ever more distant, relations seemed to thaw, with Trump even publicly mooting giving Ukraine a license to build its own Patriot missiles.
In recent weeks, however, Trump appears to have definitively ditched the US’s putative ally and sided with Putin.
Economists argue that the volume of diesel covered by his deal with Moscow is too insignificant to reduce diesel prices, which have been inflated mainly by the effects of the Iran war, rather than by the actions of Ukraine.
Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, caused further consternation by praising Putin as a “humanitarian” after the Russian president agreed to release a 74-year-old US citizen, Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia had imprisoned for several years after falsely accusing him of fighting for Ukraine.
The Russia-friendly moves have stunned Ukrainian Americans, many of whom have pro-Republican sympathies dating back to the cold war, when staunchly anti-communist presidents like Ronald Reagan were seen as champions of self-determination for the constituent, so-called “captive nations” that comprised the Soviet Union, which included Ukraine.
“We are befuddled and upset by what’s going on,” said Andrij Chornodolsky, chair of the senior citizens association, who urged his fellow members to call the White House and leave comments criticizing the recent policy moves. “How can you be doing this to us?”
The US is “helping a country that wants to subjugate Ukraine back into a new empire, the Russian empire”, added Chornodolsky, who was equally angry with Republicans who have failed to criticize Trump over his abandonment of Ukraine.
“What are the comments coming out of Congress?” he said. “Silence speaks very loudly. If you do nothing, you agree with the person making the pronouncements.”
There are about 60,000 people of Ukrainian descent in Philadelphia’s metropolitan area, the second-largest such ethnic population in the US after New York. From 105,000 to 122,000 people are estimated to claim Ukrainian ancestry throughout Pennsylvania.
Peter and Orysia Hewuka, long-term Republicans who had both previously voted for Trump, said they were likely to vote for a local Democrat because of Ukraine, even though it represented a psychological hurdle.
“I am very hesitant to vote Democrat. I’m a lifelong Republican,” said Peter, 88, a retired nuclear physicist. “But I can’t vote for people who support what Trump is doing. The Republican party has left us, we haven’t left the Republican party.
“It’s very difficult for me and for a lot of Ukrainian Americans to vote for the Republican party based on what they’ve been doing in the past months.”
Luciw, of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, said even Trump’s diehard supporters in the Ukrainian community had been alienated by the diesel deal with Putin.
Donald Trump departs a campaign rally at Ohio University Chillicothe on 28 October. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP “From my interactions on social media and elsewhere, I would say more than 75% of those who supported him have now abandoned him because it’s now clear where this is headed,” said Luciw, 68, who described himself as a Reagan Republican, but now also intends to vote Democrat.
“Until the last few weeks, there was a hope that Trump’s swinging back-and-forth on Ukraine was a kind of negotiation … that maybe he would come to terms with things because it looked liked Ukraine was going to win and he would support a winner,” he said. “But the diesel deal reversed all that.”
Mykola Hryckowian, director of the Center for US-Ukrainian Relations, said he voted for Trump three times and been active in an ad hoc group called Ukrainian Americans for Trump – but has since severed his last vestiges of support.
“I went to the polling booth in the last election not knowing who to vote for, thinking I might write in Zelenskyy, but in the end voted for Trump, because I couldn’t vote for Kamala Harris,” he recalled. “Today, I could not vote for Trump.
“But a lot of my colleagues [on the committee] were very staunch, holding onto Trump until the very end. But in these last two weeks, they have turned around and said: ‘This is an abomination’.”
Not all Ukrainians are surprised by Trump’s actions. Mark Andryczyk , a Ukrainian studies scholar at Columbia University and board member of the Ukrainian League of Philadelphia – a cultural group that hosts performances by writers and musicians from the country – said the president’s actions were predictable.
“I never thought Trump would be a good idea for Ukraine,” he said. “You just have to look at how happy Russia was each time he was elected.”
“All his information on the war is basically Russian talking points,” added Andryczyk . “I can’t imagine why anybody would think he was pulling for Ukraine. Perhaps people somehow thought that he wouldn’t be doing this. I would think that their eyes are open now.”
A clear-eyed view of Trump’s foreign policy could reap an electoral whirlwind for Trump’s Republican allies on 3 November, with the pocket-book effects of his tariffs and the war on Iran looming large as voters head to the polls.
Yet such an outcome could be a double-edged sword. Should Trump become hemmed in at home by a Democrat-controlled Congress in the final two years of his presidency, where better to assert his power than the rest of the world?

items.content:
A supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil and two other fuel ships exploded Friday when they struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz , Iran claimed.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said the supertanker burst into flames when it hit a naval mine while using an "unauthorized" route in the crucial waterway.
Three tankers exploded when they struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, Iran claimed. REUTERS
It was the third fuel tanker to strike a mine in the same day while using an illegal route in the strait — with the two other vessels exploding after switching off their navigation signals and ignoring repeated radio warnings, the Iranian guard's navy said.
Iran did not identify the ships or where they were from, nor provide details about the fate of their crews or who exactly had laid the mines.
The claims involving the damaged tankers could not be verified. The US said it has cleared all internationally recognized, primary transit routes in the strait of mines.
The reported development came as Saudi Arabia said it shot down a drone near Mecca that had been launched by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The Houthis denied the near-hit on Islam's holiest site.
This is part of the wreckage of a vessel that sank near the Strait of Hormuz and depicted in an image posted to social media Oct. 14, 2026. Social Media via REUTERS
The news meanwhile occurred as oil prices surged Friday to their highest levels since the end of April.
Oil prices could turn even more volatile over the next couple of weeks with Israel's recent elections and the US midterm elections Nov. 3 , according to a Saxo Bank briefing in Singapore.
Though it's difficult to forecast prices, crude is expected to trade in a ⁠higher range ​of $70 to $90 a barrel even after the conflict ends, compared with a pre-war range of $60 to $70, Saxo Bank said.
"Continued kinetic action around the Strait of Hormuz amidst doubts of a viable diplomatic pathway is keeping oil prices elevated in expectation of an escalation of the conflict in coming weeks," said Saul Kavonic, head of energy research at MST Marquee, to Reuters.

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
A satellite image shows Typhoon In-fa in the Pacific Ocean on Thursday. Photograph: CSU/Cira & JMA/Jaxa/Reuters Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150mph (240km/h), with winds gusting over 185mph (296km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico . Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

Markets News, Oct. 30, 2026: Tech Sell-Off Sends Nasdaq, S&P 500 Reeling; Intel Stock Drops 30%; Bitcoin Slides, Gold Hits One-Year Low
The Nasdaq Composite posted its biggest one-month decline since March of last year.
Credit: Timothy A. Clary / AFP / Getty Images Stocks plunged Friday amid mounting concerns about the health of the AI trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite and the benchmark S&P 500 ended down 2.9% and 1.8%, respectively, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.1%. The major indexes were coming off a losing session on Thursday , when the Nasdaq dropped 1.6% as a disappointing earnings report from Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) weighed on the tech sector.
The Nasdaq fell 5.3% in October, its biggest one-month decline since March 2025, when markets cratered amid concerns about the Trump administration's tariff policies. The S&P 500 fell 0.9% this month, while the Dow added 1.7%, recovering from a steep 4.3% decline in September.
Today, results from Intel (INTC) and Amazon (AMZN), released after yesterday's closing bell, dragged the market lower. Intel shares plunged 29%, leading decliners in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100, after the chipmaker issued a weak outlook that overshadowed better-than-expected third-quarter results. Amazon shares were down 1.4%, after sliding as much as 6% early in the session, as the retail and web services giant missed Wall Street expectations and reported a worrying decline in free cash flow amid massive AI spending.
Chip stocks were down sharply across the board. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Marvell Technology (MRVL) logged double-digit declines, while Broadcom (AVGO) and Micron (MU) each fell more than 5%. Shares of Nvidia (NVDA), the company at the center of the AI boom, were down 4.2% to pace Dow decliners. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), which has Intel and AMD as its two biggest holdings, fell more than 8%.
Crypto-related stocks tumbled as bitcoin traded below $77,000, down from yesterday's high near $82,000, following news of a massive hack at cryptocurrency exchange Binance. Shares of Strategy (MSTR), the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, fell nearly 8% recently, while crypto exchange Coinbase (COIN) plummeted more than 10% and trading platform Robinhood (HOOD) slid 7.2%.
In other market action, gold futures fell 3.7% to $3,883 an ounce and were trading at their lowest levels since last September. WTI oil futures climbed 2.4% to more than $104 per barrel. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which affects interest rates on loans, was down slightly unchanged from yesterday's close at 4.93%.
Go beyond the day's market moves with Investopedia's Value Add , where you'll find sharp analysis, investing ideas, and practical guidance on what today's biggest financial stories could mean for your money. Explore Value Add and subscribe on Substack .
Bitcoin Drops After Multibillion-Dollar Binance Hack
Some of that is undoubtedly related to broad softness in markets, with stocks—particularly tech shares—getting whacked. But cryptocurrency is having its own issues today , too.
Bitcoin, which earlier this year shook off its crypto-winter doldrums to clamber back over $80,000, is now below $77,000. Shares of Strategy (MSTR), a leading bitcoin buyer, were off 8%, while crypto exchange Coinbase (COIN) was down some 14%. Circle Internet Group (CRCL), a stablecoin backer, was about 11% lower.
What's going on here? You can look at Binance, another crypto exchange, which reported a "security incident" that amounts to a hack, attributed by some experts to North Koreans, that it said affected more than $6 billion. The company said it suspended withdrawals and also that all losses would be covered. "The good news is that we are recovering stolen assets for users," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X.
Those assurances have shaken confidence in crypto in a highly public fashion with The New York Times calling the event "the largest crypto heist in history." It's "a major disaster for the industry, Binance (and me)," Binance founder Changpeng Ziao, known as "CZ," wrote on X.
CZ also responded to a message on X from Elon Musk, who responded to news of the hack with an emoji denoting a grimace. "Bad time to troll," CZ replied. "Please stop."
What might happen next? "The key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly," FundStrat Head of Digital Asset Strategy Sean Farrell said in written commentary.
Binance said its U.S. trading operation was not affected by the hack, calling it a "separate, independent platform."
Gold prices are falling Friday amid lingering concerns about inflation and the prospect that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.
Gold futures were down 3.5% recently at $3,980 an ounce, trading at their lowest levels since early October 2025. Gold has lost more than a quarter of its value since hitting an all-time closing high above $5,300 in January.
Nasdaq on Track for Biggest Monthly Loss Since March 2025
The Nasdaq Composite is pacing for its worst monthly performance since early last year amid the late-week sell-off in tech stocks.
With just a few hours left in October trading, the tech-heavy index is down 5.6% for the month. If it stays at these levels, it would surpass the 4.8% loss registered in March and be the biggest decline since March of last year, when the Nasdaq fell 8.2% amid the market meltdown triggered by the Trump administration's tariff policy.
Other major indexes have turned in a mixed performance this month, with the S&P 500 down 1% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 1.8% as of mid-afternoon Friday.
Intel Stock Plunges After Chipmaker Issues Weak Outlook
The powerful recovery of Intel's stock has been one of this year's most interesting stock market stories. That story is coming apart a bit today.
Shares of Intel (INTC), which earlier this year eclipsed levels last seen in 2000 and were up roughly 250% this year through last night's close, are plummeting Friday. They were recently down 29% at $65, placing them at prices they haven't touched since the spring, and making them the morning's worst performer on the S&P 500.
The near-term culprit was last night's release of quarterly financial results. GAAP profit numbers fell year-over-year, a blow compounded by Intel's outlook.
The company pointed investors toward fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, and GAAP profits of a dime per share, all of it lower than Visible Alpha's consensus estimates. On a conference call, CEO Lip-Bu Tan acknowledged challenges in meeting "extremely high AI driven demand."
Lip-Bu Tan, seen here speaking at an event in Tokyo last month, was named CEO of Intel in March 2025.
Credit: Akio Kon / Bloomberg / Getty Images Investors have a few things to chew on in Intel's latest report, including what Tan called "headwinds across the PC industry." Some analysts continue to look for more from Intel's foundry operation, which makes chips for other companies and has been cited as a vital driver of profit growth. Foundry revenue rose nearly 60% year-over-year in Q3, but it reported an operating loss of nearly $1.9 billion.
For some, however, matters may boil down to things that were going up occasionally needing to come down. Intel recently traded at more than 50 times estimated 2027 earnings, far above the average of a peer group tracked by Visible Alpha.
Morgan Stanley analysts, who have a neutral rating on the shares, pulled their price target down to $75 from $84— Visible Alpha's mean is around $90—while observing "how expensive the stock is on next-year numbers."
Amazon (AMZN) shares dropped in early trading after the company reported quarterly results that came in short of Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines.
The company said third-quarter revenue rose nearly 12% year-over-year to nearly $202 billion. Net income fell, with the company citing a rough comparison due to gains associated with its stake in Anthropic in the year-ago-quarter.
Investors may not have liked a downturn in free cash flow driven by the company's investments in AI. Still, Amazon now projects revenue-growth run rates above 40% in 2027 and 2028 for its AWS business.
The stock was down more than 2% recently. For the year, shares are up just 3%, significantly trailing the S&P 500's 11% gain since the start of 2026.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were hovering near unchanged recently.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy greets Ukrainian soldiers in front of a Patriot anti-aircraft missile system in Germany in 2024. Photograph: Getty Images
Volodymyr Zelenskyy greets Ukrainian soldiers in front of a Patriot anti-aircraft missile system in Germany in 2024. Photograph: Getty Images
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years
The Ukrainian president called the US decision strong, but added that delivery of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠could take years
The US has approved the sale ⁠of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.
The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’
Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.
“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves ⁠of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone ​strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform ‌in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five ‌died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.
He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington ⁠after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring ‌forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, ​along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.
The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has ⁠supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, ​raising concerns about inventories of key air defense ​and precision-guided weapons.

items.summary: Hundreds of people are also understood to have stayed in the front-line town, despite the dangers.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: How will the evacuation of Oleshky unfold?
By Dan Johnson ,Â  in Kyiv ,Â  Olga Malchevska Â  and Â  Laura Gozzi
Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
"Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed the evacuees were on their way to southern Russia, from where they will travel on to Ukraine through Belarus.
Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders".
Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".
A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.
Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.
"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."
Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.
They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.
Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.
Image caption, Oleshky residents had a four-hour window to board buses to be evacuated to either Russia or Ukraine
Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.
The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.
But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Image caption, Residents travelled from Oleshky in convoy to Armyansk in Russian-occupied Crimea
Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.
In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."
Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.
"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."
Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.
"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.
"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."
Image caption, Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova spoke to journalists before arriving in Oleshky
The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.
On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.
A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.
Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

Share Oil flows are up as Iran war turmoil eases. Why do prices keep rising? on social media
Gas prices are displayed in front of a petrol station, in Carlsbad, California, US, on September 10, 2026 [Gregory Bull/AP Photo]
Oil flows out of the Gulf have increased substantially, easing the huge supply disruption caused by the United States/Israel war on Iran.
Crude exports from the Gulf averaged 24.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week to October 18, exceeding the pre-war average, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Romania extends pre-trial detention of far-right politician Calin Georgescu
list 2 of 4 UN experts sound alarm at excessive use of force in French student protests
list 3 of 4 No clear winner in Israel election with nearly 90 percent of votes counted
list 4 of 4 Israelis rally for Jewish-Arab government after election gains
Brent crude, the global benchmark, is trading at its highest prices since April, up more than 60 percent compared with before the war.
On Friday, Brent crude front-month futures – contracts for oil deliveries in December – rose more than 2 percent to briefly top $117 a barrel.
The climbing prices reflect anxiety about the possibility of renewed hostilities in the US war on Iran, dwindling oil stocks , and the increased costs of transporting supplies out of the region, according to market analysts.
“The market is doing exactly what it is supposed to do: It is telling us there is plenty of prompt oil, but there is no end to this war in sight – in fact … escalation is very likely,” Adi Imsirovic, a lecturer in energy systems at the University of Oxford, told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore, futures markets reflect that expectation,” Imsirovic, a veteran oil trader, said.
Oil producers have become increasingly adept at responding to the volatile climate in the Middle East to keep supplies flowing.
Facing the threat of Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, shipping lines have established a shuttle system involving ship-to-ship transfers off Oman and the United Arab Emirates to reduce the distance any one vessel must travel in perilous waters.
Shuttle boats carry the oil through the strait and load it onto waiting tankers once they are out of the danger zone.
In August, more than 70 percent of the crude that crossed the strait did so via ship-to-ship transfers, according to Kpler.
Oil producers have also ramped up exports that bypass the strait altogether via Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline , which carries oil supplies from its eastern oil fields to its Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the west, and the United Arab Emirates’ Habshan-Fujairah pipeline.
As of September, 40 percent of exports from the Gulf were bypassing the strait, a conduit for one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies during peacetime, compared with 17 percent before the war, according to Kpler data.
A cargo ship sails in the Gulf towards the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on October 21, 2026 [Altaf Qadri/AP] The soaring cost of delivery
Freight costs have reached as much as $40 per barrel in recent weeks, about 10 times the usual rate, according to data from the London Stock Exchange Group, the surge driven by elevated insurance premiums in addition to logistical challenges.
October has been the deadliest month for attacks on commercial vessels since the start of the war, with 32 incidents logged by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) as of Friday.
“So barrels are moving, but neither smoothly nor reliably. That should not be read as a sign of normalisation,” Isabel Figuerola-Ferretti, an expert in oil markets at Comillas Pontifical University in Madrid, Spain, told Al Jazeera.
“Delivering a barrel has become far more expensive,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.
While market intelligence data has shown exports reaching pre-war levels at various points in recent weeks, the longer-term supply trend is less clear.
Pavel Molchanov, an investment strategist at Raymond James & Associates, expressed scepticism that supply has returned to the pre-conflict trend.
“The IEA’s most recent production data – for September – shows OPEC Gulf production at 15.8 million bpd, which equates to 75 percent of the pre-war baseline,” Molchanov told Al Jazeera, referring to the International Energy Agency’s latest energy outlook.
“That slightly surpassed July’s 74 percent to reach the highest level since the start of the war, but it’s still a considerable distance from 100 percent.”
Meanwhile, oil stockpiles, a buffer during supply disruptions, are waning.
Observed inventories fell by 10 million barrels in September, taking the global stockpile to 509 million barrels below its pre-war level, according to the IEA.
“The market has moved to a chronic squeeze, driven by concrete supply risks: Hormuz transit, shipping and depleted inventories,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.
With no permanent end to the Iran war in sight, few analysts see prices returning to normal anytime soon.
Brent futures for delivery in October 2027 stood at more than $90 a barrel on Friday, in a sign that markets see normality as a long way off, still.
“When could prices return to $70? Not soon,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.
“It would need durable de-escalation, a return to normal transit and shipping conditions through Hormuz, rebuilt inventories and freight costs back to normal,” she added.
Molchanov, the investment strategist, said he did not believe supply could realistically exceed 85 percent of pre-war levels without a permanent diplomatic solution to the war.
“Once the political groundwork is in place, the next steps will be logistical: Demining Hormuz, bringing shipping crews back to work, and resuming production at currently shut-in oilfields,” he said.
