items.title: Intel Stock Suffers Worst Crash in 50 Years as Weak Forecast Overshadows AI Chip Demand - Decrypt
items.summary: Intel Stock Suffers Worst Crash in 50 Years as Weak Forecast Overshadows AI Chip Demand  Decrypt
items.content:
Intel shares plunged nearly 30% to $65.76 on Friday, wiping out more than $146 billion in market value as investors reacted to a disappointing fourth-quarter forecast.
Intel expects Q4 revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, well below Wall Street's $17.07 billion estimate, while adjusted earnings per share are forecast at $0.25 versus expectations of $0.43.
Demand for AI server processors is booming, but manufacturing and packaging shortages are limiting production. Meanwhile, Intel expects the PC market to contract through 2027 and warned it probably won't generate positive free cash flow next year.
Intel shares plunged nearly 30% to $65.76 on Friday after the chipmaker issued a fourth-quarter forecast that fell well short of Wall Street expectations, overshadowing an otherwise strong earnings report.
The selloff wiped out more than $146 billion in market value, and translated into the worst single-day decline in more than 50 years.
Myriad: Which company will IPO next? Click to make your prediction .
The problem is that Intel finds itself in an unusual position: demand for its processors is booming because of the AI infrastructure buildout, but the company cannot manufacture enough chips to capitalize on it. At the same time, its traditional PC business is struggling, and the factories needed to support its long-term recovery are consuming enormous amounts of money.
Intel's third-quarter numbers were actually quite good. Revenue climbed 21% year over year to $16.5 billion, while adjusted earnings per share reached $0.52, beating the company's guidance of $0.38 and Wall Street's $0.40 estimate. It was the company's eighth consecutive quarter of exceeding its financial expectations, according to CFO Dave Zinsner.
The strongest performer was Intel's Data Center and AI division, which generated $7.3 billion in revenue, up 78% year over year and nearly 80% compared with the same period last year. The division's operating profit reached $3 billion, representing 42% of its revenue.
But investors were looking at what comes next. Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion, meaning its midpoint guidance of $15.5 billion is roughly $1.6 billion below the $17.07 billion analysts had anticipated. Adjusted earnings per share are expected to fall to $0.25, compared with Wall Street's $0.43 estimate.
Price data by CoinGecko CoinGecko More Bitcoin news and projections →
Gross margins, which measure how much revenue remains after accounting for the direct costs of making products, are also expected to deteriorate. Intel forecast a non-GAAP gross margin of 38% for Q4, down from 44.1% in the third quarter.
Three problems explain much of that deterioration: weaker PC demand, manufacturing constraints affecting server processors, and an accident at one of Intel's factories in Israel.
Intel CFO Dave Zinsner described 2027 as an investment year and warned investors not to expect positive free cash flow. Free cash flow is the money a company has left after paying operating expenses and investments in equipment and infrastructure. Intel expects to sacrifice cash generation in the short term to finance its manufacturing expansion.
"Probably not a dynamic where we are going to have positive free cash flow next year," Zinsner said during the earnings call. He added that Intel expects a return on invested capital of at least 20% on its manufacturing node investments, but acknowledged that several major projects will require substantial spending at the same time.
That spending is part of Intel's broader attempt to rebuild its manufacturing business and compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, the world's leading contract chipmaker. Intel wants to manufacture chips not only for its own products but also for outside customers, a business model known as a foundry.
The turnaround has attracted major partners. In September 2025, Nvidia invested $5 billion in Intel and agreed to collaborate on custom processors for PCs and data centers. The partnership gave Intel a financial boost while connecting its processors to Nvidia's AI ecosystem.
Intel's next-generation 18A process, the manufacturing technology behind chips such as Panther Lake , is central to the company's attempt to regain its technological edge.
More recently, a preliminary agreement with Apple to manufacture some of its chips helped send Intel shares above $130 in May. The potential deal could give Intel a significant new customer as Apple looks to diversify its manufacturing supply chain.
Those developments helped fuel optimism around Intel's recovery, but Friday's selloff shows how much still needs to go right. The company has strong demand in its data center business, yet it must increase manufacturing output, navigate a shrinking PC market and finance an expensive expansion before investors can expect consistent cash generation.

items.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
items.summary: The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.
items.content:
By Jaroslav Lukiv Â  and Â  Joe Tidy ,Â  Cyber correspondent, BBC World Service
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist .
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (Â£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle â cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.
In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.
The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

items.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
items.summary: If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become.
items.content:
By Lily Jamali North America Technology correspondent
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack of Binance , the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.
This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.
Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.
Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.
The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.
In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.
The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".
The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.
Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.
Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected
Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.
North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.
In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.
TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.
Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.
Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become â a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.
Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.
In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.
As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

items.title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
items.summary: It is Pike's first public statement since she survived an execution attempt by lethal injection in September.
items.content:
Figure caption, The BBC's Ione Wells looks at what Christa Pike says in her statement about surviving a botched execution.
US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in the statement.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.
Image caption, Christa Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbita
She has since been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Pike is thought to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection.
I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
I interviewed Christa Pike 20 years ago - I can't stop thinking about her
What happened in Christa Pike's failed US execution, and how did she survive?
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," she said in her statement on Friday. "But healing is not the same as being okay."
Her lawyers previously said she had suffered from pneumonia following the attempted execution, had significant swelling on her arms and was also unable to swallow.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and Shipp
Pike's botched execution captivated and shocked the world last month and shocked Pike, too.
"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said in her statement.
Bethany Mann, a friend of Pike's and a founder of Child Arise Tennessee, which supports children and families affected by parental incarceration, told the BBC on Friday that she had been in direct contact with Pike since the botched execution attempt.
When asked about her reaction to Pike's statement, Mann said: "Truthfully, I don't know that I have anything to add to what Christa has already expressed so powerfully herself, and I want to be respectful of her privacy."
Figure caption, How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".
Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he responded.
Speaking about the state's response to what happened to Pike, Mann said: "I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out."
She added: "What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her."
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess".
She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology.
Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.
Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.

The EU’s foreign policy chief has accused Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov of presenting “lies” in G20 meetings in Atlanta about the Ukrainian conflict and suggested Moscow was not ready for peace negotiations . “We were talking about the big geopolitical crisis, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergei Lavrov head-on with this,” Kaja Kallas told Agence France-Presse on the sidelines of a meeting on Friday. “Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke.” Kallas said Russia did not appear ready to move ahead in peace talks. “Even if they would have said this in words, their deeds tell something else,” she said. “July, August, and September have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine.” She added: “They should show with their deeds that they are ready to negotiate, but they are clearly, clearly not.”
At the talks, which are focusing on global economic growth, energy security and trade, European officials pushed Russia to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea, an important agriculture export corridor . However, Lavrov conceded no ground on Ukraine and at a press conference, he criticised Europeans for their “arrogant boycott” while praising the willingness of US President Donald Trump’s administration to engage with Moscow.
Plans for a traditional family photo of G20 ministers were called off after some European officials objected to appearing alongside Lavrov . Moscow has been shunned by most of the West since it invaded Ukraine, and Lavrov himself remains under international sanctions. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years.” German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said there would be no photo because “there is no normality with Russia”.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio spoke briefly with Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting , with the Russian minister saying both sides had a “decent talk”. Trump has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to Florida in December and has eased some sanctions on Moscow while touting a deal for Russia to sell diesel as prices soared. The Russian foreign minister’s G20 appearance comes also ahead of fresh negotiations expected between Moscow, Kyiv and Washington in November.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration on Friday approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn , the state department said, but Ukraine’s president has warned deliveries could take years . The approval, which goes to Congress for review, comes after weeks of complaints by Ukrainian authorities that its supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling. A state department statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered but Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late Friday in a post on X that “deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS”. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
Patriot missiles are among the most important weapons Ukraine has to intercept Russian drones and missiles. The Ukrainian president on Friday suggested the US and European allies could give his country missiles they have stockpiled now , which would later be replenished by the new purchase. “We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelenskyy said.
People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation , the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war. The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River has suffered months of food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including children. A humanitarian convoy arrived in the city with food and medicine and to evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine. It’s not clear how many people chose to evacuate but US first lady Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

items.title: Reports confirm Trump’s plans to resume Iran war including strikes on civilian infrastructure - World Socialist Web Site
items.summary: Reports confirm Trump’s plans to resume Iran war including strikes on civilian infrastructure  World Socialist Web Site
items.content:
Numerous media reports and statements by government officials have confirmed that the Trump administration is preparing for a renewed war against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections. The actions being prepared include reinforcement of American forces in the region and warnings sent to Gulf allies that they should prepare for an intense military campaign.
The guided-missile cruiser USS Chosin, front, the Japanese guided-missile destroyer JS Kongo and the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt sail in formation during Keen Sword in the Philippine Sea, Oct. 21, 2026. The exercise was designed to increase readiness and interoperability between the U.S. and Japanese militaries. [Photo: Officer 2nd Class Aaron Haro Gonzalez ] On Thursday, Connecticut Democratic Senator Chris Murphy posted on X that he received a classified briefing on the plans, confirming that the White House is assembling the means for another assault that could engulf civilian infrastructure across the region.
Murphy posted the following statement on X with an accompanying video of his remarks at the Middle East Institute:
Trump is reportedly planning to restart war with Iran after the election. Some of us have been briefed on the war plan. And while I cannot disclose any details, I can say this: the plan is insane. It will not achieve objectives and will set off a new cycle of escalation.
Speaking at the institute on Wednesday, Murphy explained that legislators had discussed what renewed military operations would entail. “You’ve heard a preview that it would be a short-duration plan. I’ll just say this: their plan is insane,” adding, “It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law.”
He linked his post to reports about attacks on civilian infrastructure. Administration planners, he said, had been instructed to develop an operation whose result would be prolonged and escalating warfare. Murphy said the impact would be devastating even when measured against Washington’s own “security interests.”
Murphy’s warning is significant because he has seen the classified plans. But his invocation of a threat to America’s “commitment to the rule of law” treats its destruction as a future possibility; as though this aspect of the criminality of US imperialism has not been underway for more than two decades.
The record of military campaigns that violate US and international law run through successive Republican and Democratic administrations from the George W. Bush-era aggressive war against Afghanistan and Iraq, illegal detention and torture, and spying on the US public, to the overthrow and murder of Gaddafi in Libya and the expansion of targeted assassinations under Obama. This background places Trump’s murderous and illegal assault on Iran within the context of bipartisan criminality since the beginning of the 21st century, not as a departure from an otherwise law-abiding foreign and domestic policy.
Like all Democrats, Murphy is not opposed to the imperialist objectives behind the Trump administration’s assault on Iran. In his own words, Murphy agrees that Tehran must be prevented from obtaining a nuclear weapon and that the Islamic Republic is “responsible for the killing of thousands of Americans and unacceptable levels of support for terrorist organizations throughout the Middle East.”
The Wall Street Journal reported that Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM), briefed Trump at the White House on Thursday on military options against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine participated, alongside other cabinet members. The meeting followed a Wednesday session involving military leaders and Vice President JD Vance.
Cooper rarely briefs Trump in person. The gathering therefore marks a significant stage in the preparations. According to the Journal , Washington has told Gulf Arab governments to prepare for a “short, intense campaign” after the elections. Trump himself declared last week, “We may do another little Epic Fury,” the name of the bombing campaign that began in February.
The Pentagon has dispatched additional air defenses, ammunition and supplies while relocating personnel from vulnerable bases. An additional Patriot battery is being moved to Israel amid concerns about interceptor shortages. Bomber and fighter preparations, reductions in diplomatic staffing and the withdrawal of exposed personnel all point to preparations for Iranian retaliation as well as American attack.
Reporting identifies the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group as reinforcements expected by the end of November, potentially bringing the carrier total to three, indicating a campaign that will extend for weeks, not days.
An analysis by Lazar Berman, published by the Times of Israel and republished by the Middle East Forum, appeared under the headline that renewed war “seems inevitable.” Its argument combines tangible military preparations, Israeli pressure for joint operations and the gulf between American and Iranian negotiating positions.
Washington demands an end to Iranian enrichment, removal of enriched uranium and guarantees concerning Hormuz shipping before agreeing to substantial economic relief. Tehran demands an end to the blockade, sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and cessation of hostilities. Berman interprets these incompatible starting positions, together with Trump’s post-election freedom of action, as factors driving the renewed warfare.
Evidence of Israeli involvement was also reported by Berman who cited reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for joint strikes; that Israel prepared attacks on nuclear and energy facilities for the October 10 weekend before Trump intervened; and that Israeli lobbying continued for American participation. A confrontation between Netanyahu and military chief Eyal Zamir reportedly concerned an operation capable of triggering conflict with Iran.
The political crisis facing Netanyahu, following the October 27 Israeli elections, further intensifies the pressure for military action by the Zionist regime. Coalition political bargaining could prolong Netanyahu’s caretaker premiership, leaving him with authority despite lacking a renewed parliamentary majority.
Washington Post columnist David Ignatius reported that Vice President Vance had offered in a letter on Sunday to meet Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei personally to discuss a negotiated settlement. The report suggests Vance sought discussion of Iran’s nuclear program while acknowledging Tehran’s interests in sovereignty and economic reconstruction. Iranian media confirmed receipt of the letter, but reporting through October 30 indicated that no formal response had yet been given.
Reuters reported October 23 that two senior Iranian security officials described detailed contingency plans to attack Gulf undersea communications cables in response to a renewed assault by the US. One said Tehran would seek to prevent repairs, prolonging disruption. Revolutionary Guards official Yadollah Javani identified seven major cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz as potential targets if Iranian infrastructure were attacked.
The US-Israeli war against Iran began February 28 with strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other leadership figures. Only the previous day, Trump had publicly maintained that he had not made a final decision on force, following negotiations in Geneva. This fact exposes the unreliability of any diplomatic efforts by Washington, including assurances from Trump that the assault would not resume before the US elections.
Subsequent ceasefire announcements were at least in part repeatedly used to manipulate oil markets. Reuters documented roughly $500 million in oil trades shortly before Trump’s March 23 announcement delaying infrastructure attacks, followed by further suspicious trading before the April 7 ceasefire announcement. Its later investigation identified $7 billion in advance-positioned oil bets.
As the World Socialist Web Site has consistently maintained, the ongoing war with Iran expresses the crisis of American imperialism and its attempt to overcome political and economic contradictions through military force. The destruction already inflicted has produced neither submission nor stability, but preparations for wider attacks. The makings of a third world war lie in the logic of the expanding crisis of world capitalism, not just in Trump’s bullying and recklessness.

items.title: The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead | Mark Wolfe - The Guardian
items.summary: The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead | Mark Wolfe  The Guardian
items.content:
‘Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives.’ Photograph: John Taggart/EPA
‘Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives.’ Photograph: John Taggart/EPA
The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead
Congress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the season
H eating oil may be the clearest warning yet of how the war in Iran is deepening the US’s energy affordability crisis. Families who heat their homes with oil are facing bills that could be 50% higher this winter, adding nearly $900 to the cost of keeping their homes warm. These families were already struggling before the war began.
As the Guardian recently reported , research by my organization found that electricity shutoffs in 10 states had increased 28% over the past two years. Millions of Americans were already falling behind on their utility bills, forced to choose between paying for energy, food, medicine and rent. Now they face another round of increases in gasoline, electricity and home heating costs.
The war didn’t create America’s energy affordability crisis. But it is making a bad situation much worse.
For families living on social security, minimum-wage workers and others with little room in their budgets, higher energy prices are taking an especially heavy toll. Even middle-class families are struggling to absorb another $100 or $150 a month for gasoline, groceries and home heating.
Heating oil is the canary in the coalmine for the broader affordability crisis.
Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon Tisdall
Heating oil and diesel are essentially the same petroleum product, and both have been hit hard by the disruption to global energy markets. Higher diesel prices increase the cost of moving food, delivering goods and operating farms and construction equipment. Those costs eventually find their way into the prices families pay.
But for the millions of households that rely on heating oil, the impact is much more immediate. Unlike gasoline, which families can sometimes conserve by driving less, heating oil is essential for keeping homes warm. Families cannot simply stop filling their tanks when prices rise.
Trump described higher oil prices resulting from the war as “ a very small price to pay for USA, and world, safety and peace”. But there is nothing small about an additional $878 in heating costs for a family living on social security or working for minimum wage. The president has also said that fuel prices will fall “ like a rock ” when the war ends. I hope he is right.
Even if the war ended tomorrow, energy prices would not necessarily return to their previous levels. Damaged refineries need repairs, shipping routes must reopen, and depleted petroleum inventories need to be replenished. That could take months. Families cannot postpone paying their heating bills while the oil market recovers.
Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives. We are calling on lawmakers to add $3bn to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (Liheap), which helps low-income families pay their heating bills.
This would allow states to provide families with supplemental assistance to cover rising heating oil and electricity prices before the start of the winter heating season.
The problem extends beyond the poorest families. Many working families earn too much to qualify for assistance but still struggle to pay their energy bills. Congress should consider temporarily expanding eligibility for Liheap to struggling middle-class families, with additional funding to ensure that assistance to the lowest-income households is not reduced.
A recent survey conducted by Consumer Reports found that more than a quarter of all families reported reduced the heating and cooling in their homes to uncomfortable levels to save money and 19% cutback on groceries or switched to less expensive food options.
Without additional energy assistance, families will fall further behind, and some will face the possibility of losing heat during the coldest months of the year.
But Congress also needs to address the larger problem. For too long, we’ve measured America’s energy security by how much oil and natural gas we produce. Yet producing more energy at home hasn’t protected the US families from price shocks caused by wars overseas.
We need to think about energy security differently. That means expanding energy sources, including wind and solar, whose fuel costs cannot be driven up by a war. There is no strait of Hormuz for solar power.
That is the longer-term challenge. Right now, millions of families are heading into winter facing energy bills they cannot afford.
At some point, the war in Iran will end, but the affordability crisis will not end with it. Washington needs to help families get through this winter and make sure the next war thousands of miles away doesn’t once again determine whether they can afford to heat their homes.
Mark Wolfe is an energy economist and serves as the executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (Neada) representing the state directors of the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the co-director of the Center on Energy Poverty and Climate (CEPC). He also serves as an adjunct professor at the George Washington University public policy school

Anthony Albanese is attending Chogm and will be away when the RBA delivers its interest rate decision on Tuesday. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP
Anthony Albanese is attending Chogm and will be away when the RBA delivers its interest rate decision on Tuesday. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP
Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms
The prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda
Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast
As “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker for Anthony Albanese amid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said.
But a likely interest rate hike , triggered by higher-than-expected inflation , while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder.
Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday.
He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting.
Labor is losing control of the economic narrative as cash-strapped households look for someone to blame | Tom McIlroy
The discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies over grant funding and pressures on inflation , according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University.
“It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said.
“He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot.
“There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.”
Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.
It would be the fifth interest rate hike in 2026 and a challenging situation for the government to navigate, amid continuing cost-of-living pressures.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
Albanese emphasised the value of attending Chogm before his departure on Saturday morning. In a crowded international calendar, the Commonwealth is occasionally dismissed as irrelevant, an anachronistic relic of a former imperial era.
“The Commonwealth heads of government meeting is an important forum,” Albanese said.
“[It provides] an opportunity to work with some of our closest partners on shared challenges, including climate change, the preservation of our oceans, trade and investment and the rise of AI.”
Back to Back Barries: Is inflation driving Chalmers and Albanese apart? – podcast
The issue of historical slavery, and its ongoing legacy, is likely to be a key point of contention at Chogm.
Burnham, writing in the Guardian , said having “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future” was the right thing to do.
“Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”
He called the transatlantic slave trade a “brutal and barbaric violation” of people “treated as property and worked to their deaths”.
“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he wrote.
Caribbean nations have made renewed calls for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit, and for reparations, as the King toured the Caribbean.
Burnham said: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.” But he said he did not believe reparations for slavery was the “ right answer ”.
Australia would not be a bystander to any debate about slavery and the slave trade.
Across the 19th and early 20th centuries, Australian agriculture relied heavily on “blackbirding” : the use of coercion, trickery, bribery and kidnapping to bring more than 60,000 Pacific Islanders to work as indentured labourers in Australia, primarily on Queensland’s sugar and cotton plantations.
The Chogm meeting will kick off a busy end to the year overseas for Albanese, with international summits in Turkey, the Philippines, China and the US in coming weeks.
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is currently in Atlanta, Georgia for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting. The start of that conference has been overshadowed by the presence of Russia, with about one-third of the countries attending vowing to boycott the customary “family photo” if the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, was involved.

items.content:
If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, History Suggests These Are 2 Crucial Moves to Make.
Over the past few years, the S&P 500 has been doing something that investors appreciate. It's roared higher, and this year continues to extend the bull market. In fact, since the start of 2023, the major index has delivered a gain of 100%. This is as investors have jumped at the chance to get in on the latest big thing in technology: artificial intelligence (AI). They've bought AI stocks hand over fist, from chip designers Nvidia to memory makers like Micron Technology and cloud service providers such as Microsoft .
These companies and their peers have been generating strong revenue growth thanks to their AI products and services -- and that's prompted investors to get in on these exciting stories. All of this has led the S&P 500 higher, as AI stocks are heavily present in the benchmark. And considering that AI is in its early days of practical use, more growth could lie ahead.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
This paints a bright picture, yet some investors have started to worry about what's next for stocks -- and the words "market crash" have even emerged. But here's some good news: If a stock market crash is coming, history suggests there are two crucial moves to make.
First, let's consider the potential trouble spots investors are noticing in today's market environment. And this starts with the area of AI. Though AI stocks have pushed the index higher in recent years, investors worry that they might end up weighing on the index at a certain point. Tech giants are greatly investing in AI infrastructure, and if they overspend, earnings and their stock prices may suffer. Investors have been thinking of this risk -- and that's prompted some to hesitate before buying AI stocks or even sell their positions.
Meanwhile, though the Federal Reserve left interest rates steady during the latest meeting, higher inflation remains a concern, and the market is predicting another hike. In fact, the probability for an increase at the December meeting is at 83%, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. A higher interest rate environment generally isn't favorable for companies, as it lifts their borrowing costs, or the stock market -- higher interest rates may prompt some investors to favor bonds over stocks.
Finally, stock prices have climbed, with overall valuations at nearly record-high levels. The S&P 500 Shiller CAPE ratio, a look at stock price and earnings per share, illustrates this point.
Against this backdrop, some investors worry that a decline -- or even a market crash -- may be next. Now, it's important to note that, even if you're extremely bullish and don't believe that a crash is on the way, it's never too early to plan for a crash. These events happen periodically as part of a normal market cycle, so it's best to be prepared.
With this in mind, what should you do right now? The good news is you can take two steps to favor the growth of your portfolio -- and limit the impact of market crashes along the way. The first step is to take a long-term view when investing. This means buying stocks with the idea of holding on for a number of years, five at a minimum. When you do this, downturns or crashes may not even be noticeable in your performance down the road. History shows us the S&P 500 has always gone on to rebound from difficult times, so if you invest in strong companies, you're likely to see this same pattern.
The second thing you can do right now, and particularly during a crash, is buy stocks. Not just any stocks, but quality players at reasonable or even dirt cheap prices. In a market downturn or crash, you'll find plenty of them, and while many investors might not be in a buying mood, this actually is the best time to go shopping for stocks. Even if they fall further after your purchase, that's OK. If you aim to hold on for a number of years, you could score a big win.
So if a crash is coming -- sooner or later -- you can approach that moment with a cool head. By investing when valuations are down and focusing on the long term, you're likely to beat any of these tough moments.

items.title: Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state
items.summary: The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
items.content:
Image caption, A file photo of Joshimath town, near the site where the helicopter went missing
Five pilgrims and a pilot have died after their helicopter crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.
The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
The cause of the crash is not yet known but there had been reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.
Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.
Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.
Image caption, Badrinath is one of four temple towns along the Char Dham Yatra pilgrimage route
Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter came down near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district.
The local civil aviation authority later confirmed to Indian media that six bodies had been located.
Helicopter services have become increasingly popular among pilgrims seeking to avoid difficult mountain journeys, but their safety has come under scrutiny following a series of accidents.
Before Friday's crash, India's weather department had issued an orange alert for the area, warning of thunderstorms, hail and strong winds.
In June 2025 , seven people were killed when a helicopter carrying pilgrims crashed near Kedarnath. Another seven died in a crash on the same pilgrimage route in October 2022.
Several other helicopter accidents were reported during the 2025 pilgrimage season, prompting aviation authorities to tighten safety checks and restrict some operations.

Xi meets president of Swiss Confederation, calling for more certainty for China-Europe economic, trade cooperation
Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with President of the Swiss Confederation Guy Parmelin, who is paying a working visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang)
BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping met with President of the Swiss Confederation Guy Parmelin in Beijing on Friday, calling on both countries to inject confidence and more certainty into China-Europe economic and trade cooperation as well as into the global economic development.
Noting Switzerland is an important partner of China in Europe, Xi said Swiss cooperation with China has always been at the forefront among European countries. He added that free trade cooperation has become the brightest highlight of China-Switzerland relations, which fully demonstrates the political courage and responsibility of the two countries in adhering to open cooperation, and highlights the unique leading role of both sides in promoting the building of an open world economy.
China is willing to work with Switzerland to uphold openness, strengthen cooperation, promote a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, and jointly inject confidence and more certainty into the economic and trade cooperation between China and European countries, as well as into the global economic development, Xi said.
Since the establishment of diplomatic ties, China and Switzerland have continuously translated the China-Switzerland cooperation spirit, featuring equality, innovation and win-win results, into pragmatic outcomes, setting a model for interactions between countries of different sizes and with different social systems, Xi pointed out.
He said the two sides should respect each other, treat each other as equals, and comprehensively enhance exchanges and policy alignment at different levels.
Noting that China is accelerating the development of new quality productive forces and steadily expanding institutional opening up, Xi said the country is ready to turn its market into a market for the world and a shared market for all.
Both sides should adhere to mutual benefit and win-win results, strengthen innovation cooperation and focus on fostering cooperation in emerging industries, including digital economy, green energy storage and artificial intelligence, he added.
Xi expressed hope that Switzerland would leverage its unique influence to actively promote balanced and stable development of trade between China and European countries.
As China and Switzerland share similar positions and concepts in supporting multilateralism, Xi said both sides should deepen multilateral coordination and mutual support, firmly uphold the international system with the United Nations at its core and the international order based on international law, reform and improve the global governance system, and advance the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.
Parmelin said that since the establishment of diplomatic relations, Switzerland and China have always respected each other, maintained close high-level exchanges, and achieved fruitful cooperation results in many fields such as trade and investment, scientific research and innovation, and employment.
Noting that this year marks the 10th anniversary of the establishment of Switzerland-China innovative strategic partnership, Parmelin said that the two sides have successfully completed negotiations on signing a protocol on upgrading free trade agreement in a short period of time with high quality, demonstrating a high level of mutual trust between the two sides, which will inject new impetus into bilateral relations.
Switzerland firmly adheres to the one-China policy and looks forward to strengthening dialogue and exchanges with China, upholding mutually beneficial cooperation, and promoting greater development in cooperation in various fields, he said.
The Swiss side attaches great importance to the positive role played by China in international affairs and is willing to closely coordinate with China, adhere to multilateralism, safeguard free trade, and contribute to world development, prosperity, peace and stability, Parmelin added.
After their meeting, the two leaders witnessed the signing of the protocol on upgrading free trade agreement and multiple cooperation documents in areas like scientific research, employment and the media.
